name: Hassan Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm happy to talk. My father always said you learn more from questions than from answers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee on the continuous miner at the Ridgeback underground coal mine. The continuous miner is a big machine with a spinning drum covered in picks that cuts the coal off the face and loads it onto a shuttle car behind. I'm still on the remote control box half the time with my supervisor, Doug, watching every move, because if you cut too high you bring the roof down. I like the power of it and the way the crew works together. What wears me out is the dust mask for twelve hours and the drive back on dark roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, people just expected too much. I use AI every day, for my side business mostly, and it saves me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'm building something on the side anyway. Last year I bought a second-hand mini excavator with half my savings, and I hire myself out on weekends to farmers and builders, trenches, footings, that kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning the continuous miner, keep the weekend digging going. I'd use the AI to quote jobs, chase invoices and find work on the local buy-and-sell pages. Maybe by next year a second machine, a skid steer, if the bookings hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Half your savings on a machine is a big bet. What did your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother was worried. My father, God rest him, ran a corner grocery for thirty years, so he'd have understood. He used to say a man with his own tools never begs for work. My uncle helped me check the hours on the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the weekend work fit around twelve-hour shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my days off only. Four on, four off. It's tiring, but every job pays a bit more of the excavator back. It's nearly half paid off already.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are still useful and people just expected too much. I use AI every day for my side business and it saves me hours.
S0.think: Privately it's fine for him because he's building something on the side, a weekend mini excavator hire business bought with half his savings last year.
S0.do: Keeps learning the continuous miner and keeps the weekend digging business running, using AI to quote jobs, chase invoices and find work. Considers buying a second machine, a skid steer, next year if bookings hold.
S0.quote: He used to say a man with his own tools never begs for work.
S0.fieldNote: He is already a small business owner on his days off, which shapes everything. His late father's grocery and saying about owning your own tools are clearly a guide. His savings are partly in a machine rather than the bank, a deliberate bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for people who are willing to work and learn. Don't wait for the government or the company to save you, get moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the continuous miner will go more remote, they already run some from a chair on the surface. I'd be fine with that. But honestly, my future is the business more than the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do any training the mine offers on the remote systems, because it pays and it's good to know. I'd buy a GPS kit for the excavator, so it can dig to a design by itself, and charge more for precise work. And I'd use AI more for the business, maybe to run the bookings and the accounts completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't wait for the government. Is there anything you'd want them to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund apprenticeships, keep the roads good, and stay out of the way of small business. Every form I fill in for the excavator is an hour I'm not digging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doug, maybe. He's brilliant at feeling the roof, but he hates screens. I'd help him if he wanted, but he's proud. I understand that.

S1.say: I'd say this is an opportunity for people willing to work and learn. Don't wait for the government or the company to save you, get moving.
S1.think: Privately he expects the continuous miner to go more remote and is fine with it. His real future is the business more than the mine.
S1.do: Takes the mine's remote-systems training and buys a GPS kit so his excavator can dig to a design by itself, charging more for precise work. Uses AI to run bookings and accounts.
S1.quote: Every form I fill in for the excavator is an hour I'm not digging.
S1.fieldNote: He sees automation as something to own rather than fear, starting with GPS on his own machine. His politics are free-market but he still wants government to fund apprenticeships. He showed respect for his proud supervisor rather than pity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people should stay calm and work out where they fit. I'd tell younger guys at the mosque to learn to run the machines, not compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one scares me more. If robots can dig a trench, my excavator is just a robot that needs a driver. Two years isn't enough time to pay it off and get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd pay off the rest of the excavator fast and not buy the skid steer. I'd keep every dollar of savings. I'd look at whether I could buy or rent an automated machine and run it as a small business, being the guy who owns it rather than the guy it replaces. If the mine let me go, I'd move in with my cousin Samir's family to cut rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach goes tight thinking about the machine payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owning an automated machine needs money. Where would it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet. Maybe a loan, maybe a partnership with my uncle. Better to owe money on a robot that works than have money in the bank and nothing to do. But in two years, prices could be crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with your cousin. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. In my family, that's normal. You help family and family helps you. That's not a handout, that's how it's supposed to work.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock but people should stay calm and work out where they fit. I'd tell younger guys at the mosque to learn to run the machines, not compete with them.
S2.think: Privately this one scares him more, because a robot digging trenches turns his excavator into a robot that needs a driver. Two years isn't enough to pay it off and get ahead.
S2.do: Pays off the excavator fast, drops the skid steer plan and keeps all savings. Looks at buying or renting an automated machine to run as a business, and moves in with his cousin's family to cut rent if laid off.
S2.feel: Anxious, with his stomach tight about the machine payments.
S2.quote: Better to owe money on a robot that works than have money in the bank and nothing to do.
S2.fieldNote: His business plan is exposed here and he saw it immediately. His answer is still to own automation rather than run from it, even if it means debt. He draws a clear line between family help, which is normal, and handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build something, so build it. Don't spend five years complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is a good window for me. I can finish paying off the excavator, buy into automated gear early while it's still a new thing, and have a little business ready when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the training at the mine, pay off the excavator and get the GPS kit. By year two or three I'd leave the mine and run the business full time, maybe with two machines, one of them semi-automatic. I'd study the new systems at night with the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. It's a race and I like a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving a steady mine wage is a risk. What would make you pull back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bookings dropped for three months in a row, I'd stay at the mine longer. I'm brave, but I'm not stupid, my mother would never forgive me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When AGI fully arrives in 2031, where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not sure. Maybe as a man who owns a few machines and rents them out. Maybe even that gets squeezed. But I'd rather be the owner when it comes than the worker.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to build something, so build it. Don't spend five years complaining.
S3.think: Privately five years is a good window: pay off the excavator, buy into automated gear early, and have a small business ready when AGI arrives.
S3.do: Finishes mine training, pays off the excavator and fits GPS in the first year. Leaves the mine around year two or three to run two machines full time, one semi-automatic, and studies the new systems at night.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like a race he enjoys.
S3.quote: I'm brave, but I'm not stupid, my mother would never forgive me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits his temperament, a race he thinks he can run. He set a sensible rule for pulling back, three bad months, and joked about his mother. He admitted he doesn't know what's left for him once AGI fully arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone young who doesn't use it to build something has only themselves to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be well set up. Ten years is enough to build a proper business, maybe three or four machines, and own them outright before the robots take over the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep the mine job and the weekend work, buy the skid steer, and start learning how the automated machines are set up and serviced. Over time I'd move to owning automated gear and renting it out with a service contract. I'd probably keep a foot in the mine for the steady pay for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My mother wants me married, and with ten years I'd feel safe enough to do it soon. With two years I'd have said wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies buy everything up and there's no room for a small man. I'm not scared of the robots, I'm scared of the big boys owning all of them.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift. Any young person who doesn't use it to build something has only themselves to blame.
S4.think: Privately ten years is enough to build a proper business with three or four machines owned outright before robots take over the rest.
S4.do: Keeps the mine job and weekend work in the first year, buys the skid steer and learns how automated machines are set up and serviced. Moves over time to owning and renting out automated gear with service contracts.
S4.quote: I'm not scared of the robots, I'm scared of the big boys owning all of them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes him feel secure enough to think about marriage, which he linked directly to the timeline. His one real worry is market concentration, big companies owning all the machines. That's a free-market worry, not an anti-technology one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be caught halfway, with a machine to pay off and no time. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses to buy new equipment, and less paperwork. Give the small man a fair chance against the big companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people are building, not just what they're losing. Everyone talks about jobs disappearing, but nobody asks who's going to own the machines.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs disappearing, but nobody asks who's going to own the machines.
portrait: Hassan Haddad is 27 and trains on the continuous miner at the Ridgeback underground coal mine, still working under his supervisor Doug's close eye. He is single, and last year spent half his savings on a second-hand mini excavator that he hires out on his days off, using AI every day to run the business. His late father's corner grocery and his family and mosque shape his belief in owning your own tools and helping family. He's calm in the plateau and steady pictures, anxious when AGI in two years threatens his machine payments, and grows more confident with five and ten years as he plans to own automated machines rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be caught halfway with a machine to pay off and no time to get ahead.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small businesses to buy new equipment and less paperwork, so small operators get a fair chance against big companies.
